theory.intro: A **primitive** of $f(x)$ is a function $F(x)$ whose derivative is $f(x)$, so $F'(x)=f(x)$. Finding a primitive reverses differentiation. Constants vanish when you differentiate, so every primitive of $f$ has the form $F(x)+C$.
facts: To test a candidate, differentiate it and check whether you get $f(x)$ back.
Any two primitives of the same function differ only by a constant.
The **general primitive** of $f(x)$ is $F(x)+C$, where $C$ is the **constant of integration**.
A function whose derivative is zero everywhere is a constant function.
If $F(x)$ is a primitive of $f(x)$, then $kF(x)$ is a primitive of $kf(x)$.
If $F(x)$ and $G(x)$ are primitives of $f(x)$ and $g(x)$, then $F(x)+G(x)$ is a primitive of $f(x)+g(x)$.
The power rule for primitives, $\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}$, fails at $n=-1$ because dividing by $n+1$ would divide by zero.
steps: State whether $F(x)$ is a primitive, and add $+C$ for the general primitive

foundation.question_text: Show that $F(x)=x^{5}$ is a primitive of $f(x)=5x^{4}$.
Is $F(x)=x^{3}$ a primitive of $f(x)=x^{2}$? Justify your answer by differentiating.
foundation.solution_text:
$F(x)=x^{3}$
$F'(x)=3x^{2}$
$\ne x^{2}$
No, $F'(x)$ is $3$ times $f(x)$, so $F(x)=x^{3}$ is not a primitive of $f(x)=x^{2}$.

foundation.question_text: Show that $F(x)=x^{4}-9$ is a primitive of $f(x)=4x^{3}$.
One primitive of $f(x)=6x^{2}$ is $F(x)=2x^{3}$. Write the general primitive of $f(x)$.
foundation.solution_text:
$F(x)=2x^{3}$
Every primitive of $f(x)$ differs from $F(x)$ by a constant.
General primitive $=2x^{3}+C$

foundation.question_text: Differentiate $g(x)=x^{3}+11$ and $h(x)=x^{3}-4$. What does this show about the primitives of $3x^{2}$?
foundation.solution_text:
$g(x)=x^{3}+11$
$g'(x)=3x^{2}$
$h(x)=x^{3}-4$
$h'(x)=3x^{2}$
Both $g$ and $h$ are primitives of $3x^{2}$, so the primitives of $3x^{2}$ are not unique and differ by a constant.

foundation.question_text: A function $F(x)$ satisfies $F'(x)=0$ for every value of $x$. What kind of function is $F(x)$?
foundation.solution_text:
$F'(x)=0$
Only a constant has a derivative of zero everywhere.
$F(x)=C$

foundation.question_text: A primitive of $x^{n}$ is $\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}$. Which value of $n$ can this rule not be used for, and why?
foundation.solution_text:
$\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}$
The rule fails when $n+1=0$.
$n=-1$
At $n=-1$ the rule would divide by zero, so it cannot be used for $f(x)=x^{-1}$.

foundation.question_text: $F(x)=x^{6}$ is a primitive of $f(x)=6x^{5}$. Use this to write a primitive of $30x^{5}$.
foundation.solution_text:
$30x^{5}=5\times 6x^{5}$
A primitive of $kf(x)$ is $k$ times a primitive of $f(x)$.
Primitive $=5\times x^{6}$
$=5x^{6}$

development.question_text: Show by differentiating that $F(x)=-\dfrac{1}{x}$ is a primitive of $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x^{2}}$.
Use the chain rule to show that $F(x)=(2x-5)^{4}$ is a primitive of $f(x)=8(2x-5)^{3}$.
development.solution_text:
$F(x)=(2x-5)^{4}$
Differentiate using the **chain rule**.
$F'(x)=4(2x-5)^{3}\times 2$
$=8(2x-5)^{3}$
$=f(x)$
So $F(x)=(2x-5)^{4}$ is a primitive of $f(x)=8(2x-5)^{3}$.

development.question_text: Which of $x^{2}$, $x^{2}+7$ and $2x^{2}$ are primitives of $f(x)=2x$?
development.solution_text:
$\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^{2})=2x$
$\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^{2}+7)=2x$
$\dfrac{d}{dx}(2x^{2})=4x$
Both $x^{2}$ and $x^{2}+7$ are primitives of $f(x)=2x$, but $2x^{2}$ is not.

development.question_text: One primitive of $f(x)=8x^{3}+3$ is $F(x)=2x^{4}+3x$. Write the general primitive of $f(x)$, showing the check by differentiation.
development.solution_text:
$F(x)=2x^{4}+3x$
$\dfrac{d}{dx}(2x^{4}+3x)=8x^{3}+3$
The derivative of a constant is $0$, so adding $C$ does not change this.
General primitive $=2x^{4}+3x+C$

development.question_text: $P(x)=x^{3}-2x$ and $Q(x)=x^{3}-2x+9$. Explain why $P$ and $Q$ must be primitives of the same function.
development.solution_text:
$Q(x)-P(x)=9$
A constant has derivative $0$.
$Q'(x)-P'(x)=0$
So $Q'(x)=P'(x)$, which means $P$ and $Q$ are primitives of the same function.

development.question_text: The functions $u(x)$ and $v(x)$ satisfy $u'(x)=v'(x)$ for every value of $x$. What can you say about $u(x)-v(x)$?
development.solution_text:
$\dfrac{d}{dx}(u(x)-v(x))=u'(x)-v'(x)$
$=0$
A function with derivative zero everywhere is constant.
$u(x)-v(x)=C$

development.question_text: For which one of $f(x)=x^{4}$, $f(x)=x^{-3}$, $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x}$ and $f(x)=x^{\frac{1}{2}}$ can the power rule for primitives not be used?
development.solution_text:
The power rule fails only when $n=-1$.
$x^{4}$ has $n=4$
$x^{-3}$ has $n=-3$
$\dfrac{1}{x}=x^{-1}$, so $n=-1$
$x^{\frac{1}{2}}$ has $n=\dfrac{1}{2}$
The rule cannot be used for $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x}$.

development.question_text: $F(x)=x^{7}$ is a primitive of $7x^{6}$ and $G(x)=x^{3}$ is a primitive of $3x^{2}$. Write a primitive of $7x^{6}+3x^{2}$ and verify it.

mastery.question_text: Show that $F(x)=x^{2}(x-3)$ is a primitive of $f(x)=3x^{2}-6x$.
mastery.solution_text:
$F(x)=x^{2}(x-3)$
Differentiate using the **product rule**.
$F'(x)=2x(x-3)+x^{2}(1)$
$=2x^{2}-6x+x^{2}$
$=3x^{2}-6x$
$=f(x)$
So $F(x)=x^{2}(x-3)$ is a primitive of $f(x)=3x^{2}-6x$.

mastery.question_text: A student says that because $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^{8})=8x^{7}$ and $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^{8}-3)=8x^{7}$, the function $8x^{7}$ has exactly two primitives. Explain the error.
mastery.solution_text:
$\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^{8}+C)=8x^{7}$ for every constant $C$.
Each different value of $C$ gives a different primitive.
So $8x^{7}$ has infinitely many primitives, and its general primitive is $x^{8}+C$.

mastery.question_text: $F(x)$ is a primitive of $f(x)$ and $G(x)$ is a primitive of $g(x)$. Explain why $4F(x)-G(x)$ is a primitive of $4f(x)-g(x)$.
mastery.solution_text:
$\dfrac{d}{dx}(4F(x)-G(x))=4F'(x)-G'(x)$
$=4f(x)-g(x)$
Differentiating $4F(x)-G(x)$ returns $4f(x)-g(x)$, so it is a primitive of $4f(x)-g(x)$.
